title: Part 2, Chapter 26
paragraphs: In which the comical adventure of the puppet showman continues, along with other things that are genuinely worth the telling

All fell silent, Tyrians and Trojans alike — by which I mean that everyone watching the show was hanging on the lips of the boy who explained its marvels — when drums and trumpets were heard sounding inside it and artillery going off. The noise quickly died away, and then the boy raised his voice and said, “This true history presented here before your worships is taken word for word from the French chronicles and from the Spanish ballads that are on everyone’s lips, even the lips of the boys in the streets. It tells how Señor Don Gaiferos rescued his wife Melisendra, who was held captive in Spain by the Moors in the city of Sansueña — for that was the name then given to what is now called Saragossa. And there you may see Don Gaiferos playing at the gaming tables, just as the song goes—
At the tables Don Gaiferos sits at play, For Melisendra is forgotten now.

And that figure you see there, with a crown on his head and a scepter in his hand, is the Emperor Charlemagne, said to be Melisendra’s father, who, furious at his son-in-law’s idleness and indifference, comes in to scold him. Notice how vehemently and forcefully he rebukes him — you would swear he was about to land half a dozen raps on him with that scepter; and in fact there are authors who say he did land them, and solid ones too. And after telling him at length how he was putting his honor at risk by failing to win his wife’s release, he said, as the tale has it,
I’ve said enough — now see to it.

Notice, too, how the emperor turns his back and leaves Don Gaiferos seething; and now watch how, in a burst of rage, he hurls the table and the gaming board away from him and calls urgently for his armor, and asks his cousin Don Roland to lend him his sword, Durindana; and how Don Roland refuses to lend it, offering instead to join him in the difficult enterprise he is undertaking. But the valiant, angry Gaiferos will not accept the offer, declaring that he alone is enough to rescue his wife, even if she were locked away in the deepest center of the earth; and with that he goes off to arm himself and start his journey at once. Now turn your eyes, your worships, to that tower appearing over there, which is meant to be one of the towers of the alcazar of Saragossa, known today as the Aljaferia; and that lady appearing on the balcony, dressed in Moorish fashion, is the peerless Melisendra, who many a time would gaze from there toward the road to France, consoling herself in her captivity with thoughts of Paris and her husband. Now watch a fresh incident, the like of which has perhaps never been seen before. Do you not see that Moor who, silently and stealthily, finger to his lips, creeps up on Melisendra from behind? See how he plants a kiss right on her lips, and how quickly she spits and wipes them with the white sleeve of her smock, and how she laments and tears her lovely hair, as if it were to blame for the offense. Notice also that stately Moor standing in that corridor: he is King Marsilio of Sansueña, who, having witnessed the Moor’s insolence, immediately orders him — even though the man is his kinsman and a great favorite — to be seized and given two hundred lashes while being paraded through the streets of the city in the customary way, with criers walking ahead of him and officers of justice behind. And here you see them coming out to carry out the sentence, although the crime has barely been committed; for among the Moors there are no indictments or remands as there are with us.”

At this point Don Quixote called out, “Child, child, get on with your story in a straight line and don’t go wandering into curves and tangents, for to establish a fact beyond doubt takes a great deal of proof and corroboration.” And from inside Master Pedro said, “Boy, stick to your text and do as the gentleman tells you; that’s the soundest course. Keep to your plainsong and don’t attempt counterpoint, for fancy harmonies have a way of breaking down from being too refined.”

“I will,” said the boy, and he continued, “This figure you see here on horseback, wrapped in a Gascon cloak, is Don Gaiferos himself. His wife, now avenged for the insolence of the lovesick Moor, has taken her place on the balcony of the tower with a calmer, more settled expression, and has caught sight of him without recognizing him; and taking her husband for some passing traveler, she speaks to him and holds with him the whole conversation and exchange of the ballad that runs—
If you, sir knight, are bound for France, Oh! ask there for Gaiferos—

—which I will not repeat here, since long-windedness breeds boredom. It is enough to see how Don Gaiferos reveals who he is, and how Melisendra’s joyful gestures show us that she has recognized him; and what is more, we now see her lowering herself from the balcony to seat herself on the haunches of her good husband’s horse. But ah, unlucky lady! the hem of her petticoat has snagged on one of the balcony’s bars, and she is left hanging in midair, unable to reach the ground. But see how merciful heaven sends help in our worst moments of need: Don Gaiferos rides up and, without caring whether the rich petticoat tears or not, takes hold of her and hauls her down to the ground by force; then with a single heave he sets her on his horse’s haunches, astride like a man, and tells her to hold on tight and wrap her arms around his neck, crossing them over his chest so she will not fall, since the lady Melisendra was not accustomed to riding that way. See, too, how the horse’s neighing shows how pleased he is with the gallant and beautiful burden he carries in his lord and lady. See how they wheel about and leave the city behind, and how joyfully and gladly they take the road to Paris. Go in peace, O peerless pair of true lovers! May you arrive safely in the homeland you long for, and may fortune set no obstacle in the way of your happy journey; may the eyes of your friends and kinsmen see you living out the rest of your days in peace and quiet — and may those days be as many as Nestor’s!”
Here Master Pedro called out again: “Simplicity, boy! None of your flights of fancy — all affectation is bad.”

The interpreter made no reply but went on: “There was no shortage of idle eyes — the kind that see everything — to watch Melisendra climb down and mount up, and word was carried to King Marsilio, who at once ordered the alarm to be sounded; and see what an uproar there is, and how the city is drowned in the sound of the bells pealing from the towers of all the mosques.”

“No, no,” said Don Quixote at this point; “on the matter of the bells Master Pedro is badly mistaken, for the Moors do not use bells, only kettledrums and a kind of small trumpet rather like our clarion; ringing bells like this in Sansueña is without question a great absurdity.”

Hearing this, Master Pedro stopped the ringing and said, “Don’t fuss over trifles, Señor Don Quixote, or demand a level of perfection that is beyond reach. Aren’t a thousand plays performed all around us almost every day, stuffed with thousands of errors and absurdities, and yet they run successfully and are received not only with applause but with admiration and everything else besides? Carry on, boy, and pay no attention; as long as I fill my purse, I don’t care if I show as many blunders as there are motes in a sunbeam.”

“Fair enough,” said Don Quixote; and the boy went on: “See what a numerous and glittering troop of horsemen rides out of the city in pursuit of the two faithful lovers — what a blaring of trumpets, what a sounding of horns, what a beating of drums and tabors! I fear they will overtake them and drag them back tied to the tail of their own horse, which would be a dreadful sight.”

Don Quixote, however, seeing such a swarm of Moors and hearing such a racket, decided it would be right to help the fugitives; and rising to his feet he cried out in a loud voice, “Never, as long as I live, will I allow foul play to be done in my presence against so famous a knight and so fearless a lover as Don Gaiferos. Halt, low-born rabble! Do not follow or pursue him, or you will have me to fight!” And matching deed to word, he drew his sword, leapt in a single bound right up to the show, and with unheard-of speed and fury began raining blows down on the puppet troop of Moors, toppling some, beheading others, crippling this one and smashing that one; and among many other strokes he delivered one downward cut which, if Master Pedro had not ducked, made himself small, and scrambled out of the way, would have sliced his head off as easily as if it had been made of marzipan. Master Pedro kept shouting, “Stop, Señor Don Quixote, stop! Can’t you see that these things you’re knocking down, killing, and destroying aren’t real Moors but only little pasteboard figures? Look — sinner that I am! — you’re wrecking and ruining everything I own!” But for all that, Don Quixote never stopped delivering a continuous shower of cuts, slashes, downstrokes, and backstrokes, and in the end, in less time than it takes to say two credos, he brought the whole show crashing to the ground, with all its fittings and figures hacked and broken to pieces, King Marsilio gravely wounded, and the Emperor Charlemagne split in two, crown and head together. The entire audience was thrown into an uproar; the ape fled to the roof of the inn; the cousin took fright; and even Sancho Panza himself was mightily afraid, for — as he swore once the storm had passed — he had never seen his master in such a furious rage.

With the show thus completely demolished, Don Quixote calmed down somewhat and said, “I wish I had standing before me right now all those who do not believe, or will not believe, how useful knights-errant are in the world. Just consider: if I had not been present here, what would have become of the brave Don Gaiferos and the fair Melisendra? You may be certain those dogs would have caught up with them by now and done them some outrage. When all is said, then — long live knight-errantry, above everything alive on earth today!”
“Let it live and welcome,” said Master Pedro at this, in a feeble voice, “and let me die, for my luck is so bad that I can say with King Don Rodrigo—
Yesterday I was lord of Spain; today I have not a single turret left that I can call my own.

Not half an hour ago — no, barely a minute — I saw myself master of kings and emperors, my stables full of countless horses and my trunks and sacks crammed with fine costumes beyond numbering; and now I find myself ruined and brought low, destitute and a beggar, and worst of all without my ape, for by my faith my teeth will have to sweat before I get him caught again. And all because of the reckless fury of this sir knight here, who is said to shelter orphans, right wrongs, and do other works of charity — yet in my case alone his generous intentions came up short, blessed and praised be highest heaven! Truly he must be the Knight of the Rueful Figure, to have so disfigured mine.”

Sancho Panza was moved by Master Pedro’s words and said to him, “Don’t weep and carry on so, Master Pedro; you’re breaking my heart. Let me tell you that my master, Don Quixote, is so catholic and scrupulous a Christian that if he comes to see he has done you any wrong, he will admit it and be glad to pay for it and make it good — with something extra on top.”

“If Señor Don Quixote would only pay me for some part of the work he has destroyed,” said Master Pedro, “I would be satisfied, and his worship would set his conscience at rest; for no one can be saved who keeps what belongs to another against the owner’s will and makes no restitution.”
“That is true,” said Don Quixote; “but so far, Master Pedro, I am not aware of having anything of yours.”

“What!” Master Pedro shot back. “And these relics lying here on the bare hard ground — what scattered and shattered them but the invincible strength of that mighty arm? And whose were the bodies they belonged to but mine? And how did I earn my living except by them?”

“Now I am fully convinced,” said Don Quixote, “of something I have believed many times before: that the enchanters who persecute me do nothing but set figures like these before my eyes and then change and transform them into whatever they please. In all truth and earnest, gentlemen, I assure you who hear me now that everything that took place here seemed to me to be taking place literally — that Melisendra was Melisendra, Don Gaiferos Don Gaiferos, Marsilio Marsilio, and Charlemagne Charlemagne. That is why my anger was stirred; and to be true to my calling as a knight-errant I sought to give aid and protection to the fleeing pair, and with that good intention I did what you saw. If it has turned out the opposite of what I intended, the fault is not mine but that of the wicked beings who persecute me. Even so, I am willing to sentence myself to pay the costs of this mistake of mine, though it did not spring from malice: let Master Pedro say what he wants for the ruined figures, and I will pay it on the spot in good, current money of Castile.”

Master Pedro bowed to him and said, “I expected nothing less from the rare Christian spirit of the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha, true helper and protector of all destitute and needy wanderers. Let master landlord here and the great Sancho Panza act as arbitrators and appraisers between your worship and me of what these battered figures are worth, or might be worth.”

The landlord and Sancho agreed, and Master Pedro then picked up from the floor King Marsilio of Saragossa, minus his head, and said, “You can see for yourselves how impossible it is to restore this king to his former condition; so I think — subject to your better judgment — that for his death, decease, and demise I should be given four reals and a half.”
“Go on,” said Don Quixote.
“Well then, for this split from top to bottom,” Master Pedro continued, picking up the cloven Emperor Charlemagne, “it would not be asking much if I claimed five reals and a quarter.”
“That’s not a small sum,” said Sancho.
“Nor is it a large one,” said the landlord; “split the difference and call it five reals even.”

“Give him the whole five and a quarter,” said Don Quixote, “for the grand total of this notable disaster doesn’t turn on a quarter more or less. And finish up quickly, Master Pedro, for it’s getting on toward suppertime and I’m feeling certain stirrings of hunger.”
“For this figure,” said Master Pedro, “which has lost its nose and is missing an eye, and which is the fair Melisendra, I ask — and I’m being reasonable in my price — two reals and twelve maravedis.”

“The devil himself must be in it,” said Don Quixote, “if Melisendra and her husband aren’t at least at the French border by now, for the horse they rode looked to me to be flying rather than galloping. So don’t try to sell me a cat for a hare by showing me a noseless Melisendra here, when she may well be taking her ease with her husband in France at this very moment. God help each man to his own, Master Pedro, and let us all deal plainly and honestly; and now carry on.”

Master Pedro, seeing that Don Quixote was beginning to wander and slip back into his old delusion, had no intention of letting him get away, so he said, “Then this cannot be Melisendra; it must be one of the maids who waited on her. So if I’m given sixty maravedis for her, I’ll consider myself content and well paid.”

And so he went on, setting prices on a great many more smashed figures, which, after the two arbitrators had adjusted them to the satisfaction of both parties, came to forty reals and three-quarters; and on top of that sum, which Sancho paid out at once, Master Pedro asked for two reals more for the trouble of catching the ape.

“Give them to him, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “not for catching the ape but for getting drunk; and I would give two hundred this very minute, as a reward for good news, to anyone who could tell me for certain that the lady Doña Melisandra and Señor Don Gaiferos are now in France among their own people.”

“No one could tell us that better than my ape,” said Master Pedro, “though there’s no devil who could catch him now. Still, I suspect affection and hunger will drive him to come looking for me tonight; but tomorrow will soon be here, and then we shall see.”

In short, the storm over the puppet show blew over, and everyone supped in peace and good fellowship at the expense of Don Quixote, whose generosity knew no limits. Before daylight the man with the lances and halberds took his leave, and shortly after daybreak the cousin and the page came to say goodbye to Don Quixote — the one heading home, the other continuing his journey, toward which Don Quixote gave him twelve reals to help him along. Master Pedro had no wish to get tangled in any further exchanges with Don Quixote, whom he knew all too well; so he rose before the sun, gathered up the remains of his show, caught his ape, and went off to seek his own adventures. The landlord, who did not know Don Quixote, was as astonished by his mad antics as by his generosity. To conclude, Sancho, on his master’s orders, paid him very generously, and after taking their leave of him they left the inn at about eight in the morning and took to the road, where we shall leave them to travel on; for this is necessary to make room for the telling of certain other matters that are needed to clear up this famous history.
